chunks: Probe input impedance: what and why. The question: Probe input impedance - what should it be any why?
A probe is part of the circuit while you measure. Its input impedance, how strongly it resists the signal at each frequency, decides how much it disturbs the node.
For general measurements you want the probe's impedance much higher than the node's own source impedance, about ten times or more, at every frequency that matters.
Capacitance makes that harder as frequency rises.
A huge thermometer would cool a cup of tea and read falsely. A probe must be electrically "small". At low frequency, resistance counts.
At high frequency, capacitance takes over, and a probe that looked tiny becomes a big load. For 50 ohms cables the rule flips, as the example shows.
The same node looks very different through three probes. The 1x probe is down 3 decibels at about 1.
4 megahertz, the 10x at about 13 megahertz, and the 1 picofarads active probe at about 160 megahertz (where its curve crosses the minus 3 decibels line).
A 1 kilohms node is already "high impedance" at 100 megahertz.
Impedance: the opposition a circuit gives to a signal at a given frequency, in ohms. Source impedance: the impedance the node being measured drives through.
Higher means easier to disturb. Capacitive reactance: a capacitor's opposition, 1 over (2 pi f C) . It falls as frequency rises.
10x probe: about 10 megohms in parallel with 10 to 15 picofarads.
A node has a 1 kilohms source impedance. A 10x probe's 10 megohms is far higher, so at DC the probe is harmless.
At 100 megahertz, 12 picofarads has a reactance of 1 over (2 pi times 10 to the 8 times 12 times 10 to the -12) about 133 ohms .
That is lower than the node's 1 kilohms, so the probe loads it badly.
The 1 kilohms source and the probe capacitance form a filter that starts cutting signals above about 13 megahertz, so fast edges look rounded.
An active probe with about 1 picofarads moves that point to about 160 megahertz.
For a 50 ohms cable carrying fast signals (a transmission line), the goal is different: you want a 50 ohms load at the end so no echo, or reflection, bounces back.
That is the whole idea.
"The probe impedance should be much higher than the source impedance at every frequency of interest, at least 10 times, so it doesn't load the node.
A 10x passive probe is about 10 megaohms with 10 to 15 picofarads, but at high frequency the capacitance dominates: 12 picofarads is only about 130 ohms at 100 megahertz.
For high-speed or high-impedance nodes I use an active probe with about a picofarad.
For 50 ohm transmission lines the scope's 50 ohm input is the right choice, because it terminates the line."
Quick check. For general-purpose measurements, what probe input impedance do you want relative to the circuit's source impedance?
